_note: Informal Spanish, slang and swear words in Spain (/knowledge/slang). Own draft, idioms-mistakes run (2026-11-06), not yet reviewed. reg: umgang (informal) | slang | vulgaer (rude); stufe (vulgaer only): 1 mild, 2 strong, 3 very strong. w, bsp and the hoeflich pairs are Spanish; std is the standard word with its English meaning; info is English. variety on every entry, es419 where usage differs. No slurs and no insults about groups of people (content-plan §5.7). The old law note is gone, as the plan says.

gruppen.titel: Short forms: how people really speak
gruppen.intro: In everyday speech, words get shorter. Don't write these forms in a letter or an exam, but you will hear them every day.

eintraege.bsp: Vemos una peli en la tele.
La profe de mi hijo es muy maja.
eintraege.info: profe is the normal way to speak to a teacher, in class too.
moto and foto are so common that nobody says the long form any more.

eintraege.bsp: ¿Me dejas un boli? Mi compi se ha llevado el mío.

eintraege.info: Friendly, with people you know. Not at an office.
You'll hear it often, and read it in songs. Never write it in an exam.

eintraege.bsp: Estoy cansao: he trabajao todo el día.
eintraege.info: The d between vowels often disappears in speech, above all in -ado. Very common, but keep the d when you write.

gruppen.intro: These words are relaxed, but not rude. With friends and colleagues they are normal. In a formal letter or at an office, use the word on the right.

eintraege.info: The word you'll hear most in Spain. It's fine almost everywhere, also at work.

es419.note: A marker of Spain. Latin America prefers okey, dale, bueno or está bien.

eintraege.info: Literally uncle and aunt. Among friends, and about people you don't know: un tío en el bar. Not to your boss.

es419.note: Mainly Spain. Elsewhere other words: güey in Mexico, che in Argentina.

eintraege.info: Plural: unas fotos guays. People of any age understand it.

es419.note: Mainly Spain. Elsewhere: chévere, padre, bacán, depending on the country.

eintraege.std: me gusta, es estupendo (I like it, it's cool)
eintraege.info: Works like gustar: me mola, me molan.

eintraege.std: trabajar, el trabajo (to work, the job)
eintraege.info: Very common among colleagues. In an interview: trabajar.

eintraege.std: sorprenderse mucho (to be amazed, not to believe it)
eintraege.bsp: Flipé con el precio del alquiler.
eintraege.info: Good or bad surprise. ¡Estás flipando! means you've lost touch with reality.

eintraege.std: vamos, de acuerdo, adiós (come on, OK, bye)
eintraege.info: At the end of a phone call, venga, venga means OK, bye.
Said to women too. It doesn't refer to any man.

eintraege.std: no, en absoluto (no way, not at all)
eintraege.info: A friendly, strong no.
Typical of Spain, and always a compliment.

eintraege.bsp: Cojo el autobús a las ocho.
eintraege.info: Completely normal in Spain, and not slang.

es419.note: In Mexico, Argentina and other countries coger is vulgar (= to have sex). Use tomar there.

gruppen.intro: In class you learn the normal words. You will still hear these a lot: you need to understand them, but you don't have to say them.

eintraege.bsp: No tengo pasta para el viaje.
eintraege.info: Not only the food! Very common among friends.

es419.note: Mainly Spain. Elsewhere often: la plata, la lana.

eintraege.info: Among friends, not in shops.

eintraege.bsp: El coche me ha costado un pastón.

eintraege.info: Usually two people, half each. In a group: a escote.

eintraege.bsp: Diez euros por un café: ¡vaya clavada!
eintraege.info: Also the verb: en ese bar te clavan.

eintraege.std: y algo más (… and a bit)
eintraege.bsp: Son las ocho y pico. Tiene cuarenta y pico años.
eintraege.info: After numbers and times. Careful: in some Latin American countries pico is rude.

es419.note: In Chile and parts of the Americas pico is vulgar. y algo is safer there.

eintraege.bsp: Volvimos a casa a las tantas.
Hay un porrón de gente en la cola.
eintraege.info: Literally, a glass wine jug with a spout.

gruppen.intro: Slang changes fast. Young people use it with each other. An adult who uses it at the office often sounds strange.

eintraege.std: como, más o menos (like, sort of)
eintraege.bsp: Estaba en plan: no me lo creo.
eintraege.info: Young people use it all the time, as English speakers use like.

eintraege.bsp: Me gusta mazo. Está mazo bien.
eintraege.info: Typical of young people, above all in Madrid. Understand it, don't use it at work.

eintraege.std: el tema, el ambiente (the thing, the vibe)
eintraege.bsp: ¡Qué rollo de reunión! Aquí hay buen rollo.
eintraege.info: qué rollo = how boring. buen rollo = a good atmosphere.
Means to get something, or to get a joke. Also: me pilla lejos = it's far for me.

eintraege.bsp: Este barrio es un poco chungo de noche.
eintraege.info: Also for an illness or a hard exam.

eintraege.std: de mala calidad, barato y feo (cheap and nasty)
eintraege.info: Doesn't change for gender: un bar cutre, una tienda cutre.

eintraege.bsp: Mi hermano es un friki de los videojuegos.
eintraege.info: It can be affectionate. People use it about themselves too.

eintraege.bsp: Lo has arreglado en un minuto: ¡eres un crack!
eintraege.info: From football. It works for a woman too: Ana es una crack.

eintraege.bsp: De joven hacía pellas los viernes.
eintraege.info: Other parts of Spain have other words for it, such as hacer novillos.

eintraege.std: dar vergüenza ajena (to make you cringe)
eintraege.info: From English. The standard way to say it is vergüenza ajena: being embarrassed on someone else's behalf.

gruppen.intro: You'll hear swear words more often in Spain than in many countries, even on TV and at work. You should understand them, but saying them yourself is risky: as a foreigner you can quickly sound aggressive.

eintraege.info: The polite form of hostia. Fine in almost any company.
The polite form of joder. Even children say it.

eintraege.bsp: Me he dado una leche con la moto.
eintraege.info: Yes, literally milk. Rude only in a mild way.
Extremely common in Spain, and among friends hardly noticed. Not with a client, a doctor or a civil servant.

es419.note: The exclamation sounds typically Spanish. In Latin America joder is mainly a verb (to annoy, to ruin), and how rude it is varies by country.

eintraege.info: Literally the communion wafer, so it can offend religious people. Una hostia is also a hard hit.
Common, but rude. Not at work or in front of children.

eintraege.bsp: El capullo del coche de delante no se mueve.
eintraege.info: An insult when you say it to someone's face.

eintraege.std: algo muy aburrido o molesto (a real pain)
eintraege.info: Very common, and it comes from a rude word for the female body. Avoid it in polite company.

eintraege.std: persona muy estúpida (a real idiot, an asshole)
eintraege.info: A strong insult. Said to someone's face, it can start a fight.

eintraege.bsp: ¡Qué cabrón, me ha quitado el sitio!
eintraege.info: Literally a billy goat. Among close friends it can be friendly, but you can't tell when as a learner.
You'll hear it when someone is furious. Never say it: the words after it often name someone's family or religion.

eintraege.std: Vete, déjame en paz. (Go to hell)
eintraege.info: You'll hear it in films and in fights. Never use it at work, with strangers or with the police.
It insults someone's mother, so don't ever say it. Understand it so that you know how serious the situation is.

hoeflich.zu: ¿Puedes bajar un poco la voz, por favor?
